title: Filter samples with Q15 coefficients
audience: Students with basic programming knowledge learning assembly
prerequisites: Scalar loops and MSA lane operations
learningObjectives: Define Q15 scale and chronological order
Widen before vector dot products and compare work

inputDomain.rounding: nearest, ties toward positive infinity, once after exact accumulation

progression.localImplementation: Native prose and public CLI checks; interactive runner and actual capture pending

steps.title: Identify the current sample in the supplied input

quiz.prompt: Which array position is current for output zero?

choices.text: Zero.
Seven.
Eight.

hints.text: Read the input as seven chronological history samples followed by the new samples.
One output requires eight input halfwords, two output bytes and the same sixteen coefficient bytes used by every output.

completion.reason: Reasoning and IDE interaction require review; interactive runner pending.

steps.title: Predict an asymmetric impulse response

quiz.prompt: Which stored coefficient determines the first impulse output?

choices.text: The last coefficient, position seven.
The first coefficient, position zero.
The sum of every coefficient regardless of impulse position.

hints.text: First use the default impulse 16000 with all coefficients 4096: eight outputs are 2000 and later outputs zero.
The unequal-coefficient response is 4096,3584,3072,2560,2048,1536,1024,512, then zeros.

completion.reason: Reasoning and IDE interaction require review; interactive runner pending.

steps.title: Inspect the two entries and provisional exits

quiz.prompt: Does the initial transfer require a nested-call return address?

choices.text: Only for count zero.
Yes; every label transition changes ra.
No; the branch preserves the original caller continuation.

hints.text: The starter’s public fir_q15 entry tail-transfers to fir_scalar with an ordinary branch, preserving the caller’s ra.
The untouched starter assembles and exits but fails final filtering. A provisional return reports only the construction reached so far.

completion.reason: Reasoning and IDE interaction require review; interactive runner pending.

steps.title: Guard the output count before reading history

quiz.prompt: May an empty call load the coefficients merely because their sixteen bytes exist?

choices.text: No; the zero-output contract forbids caller-data access.
Yes; coefficients are always read-only.
Only when the history is zero.

hints.text: The public entry initially transfers directly to fir_scalar without changing ra.
The zero-output recipe returns v0=0 and v1=0 without a caller-data read or write.

steps.title: Start one complete eight-tap window

quiz.prompt: Which address should advance only once per output?

choices.text: The coefficient base after every output.
The caller’s return address.
The outer window base a0.

hints.text: Clear t0 for the exact sum, copy the outer input address into t1 and the coefficient address into t2, then set the tap count in t3 to eight.
Before the first tap, t0=0 and t3=8. The two walkers identify the selected input and coefficient starts.

steps.title: Load the oldest sample in this window

quiz.prompt: Which sample does tap zero multiply?

choices.text: The oldest sample of the selected window.
The sample after the window.
The first new sample regardless of window position.

hints.text: Use two unsigned byte loads from t1.
For sample -1000, t4=24 and t5=252, the stored hexadecimal bytes 18 fc.

steps.title: Join the sample’s low and high bytes

quiz.prompt: What has the OR produced?

choices.text: An input address advanced by eight.
The unsigned sixteen-bit sample pattern.
A complete weighted product.

hints.text: Shift the high byte left by eight and OR it into the low byte.
The worked negative sample has unsigned halfword pattern 64536 in t4.

steps.title: Extend the sample before multiplication

quiz.prompt: Which bit supplies the extension?

choices.text: Bit fifteen of the reconstructed sample.
The sign bit of the input address.
Bit seven of the low byte.

hints.text: Use seh so the halfword sign bit determines the complete signed register value.
t4 is -1000 for the negative recipe and 32767 for the positive boundary recipe.

steps.title: Load the matching Q15 coefficient

quiz.prompt: Why may t5 be reused here?

choices.text: All coefficients are positive.
Loading a coefficient stores the sample automatically.
The signed sample no longer depends on its former high-byte temporary.

hints.text: Read two bytes from t2 into t5 and t6.
Coefficient -16384 has low byte zero and high byte 192. The signed sample -1000 remains in t4.

steps.title: Reconstruct the coefficient code

quiz.prompt: Does the Q15 scale reverse the stored bytes?

choices.text: Yes; fractional values use the high byte first.
Only for negative coefficients.
No; the contract still stores the low byte first.

hints.text: Shift t6 left by eight and combine it into t5.
Coefficient bytes 00 c0 reconstruct unsigned pattern 49152 in t5.

steps.title: Give the coefficient its signed value

quiz.prompt: Why not divide the coefficient by 32768 at this point?

choices.text: That would discard the fractional weight before the product.
The coefficient is already a full address.
Every coefficient represents an integer greater than one.

hints.text: Sign-extend the coefficient halfword with seh.
t5 is -16384 in the negative-coefficient recipe and 16384 in the positive recipe.

steps.title: Form the exact signed product

quiz.prompt: Which value still contains the pre-add accumulator?

hints.text: Multiply the two sign-extended values with dmul and retain the product in t7.
The worked product is 16384000. Two minimum codes produce 1073741824 for one product. The accumulator is still zero.

steps.title: Add the product without narrowing the sum

quiz.prompt: Why use a doubleword addition even though one product fits a word?

choices.text: It makes rounding unnecessary.
It permits reading beyond the input window.
The complete and partial sums may exceed signed word range.

hints.text: Add t7 into t0 using daddu.
The first worked contribution leaves t0=16384000 and t3=8.

steps.title: Consume exactly eight matched pairs

quiz.prompt: Where does the coefficient walker begin for the next output?

choices.text: At the unchanged coefficient base.
Sixteen bytes beyond the coefficient array.
At the destination byte after the last store.

hints.text: Advance both private walkers by two, decrement t3 and repeat scalar_tap while a pair remains.
Eight minimum/minimum products leave exact t0=8589934592 and t3=0. Eight sample-one, half-weight products leave t0=131072. Both walkers advance sixteen bytes.

steps.title: Add half a scale unit once

quiz.prompt: How many times is this bias added per output?

choices.text: Once for the entire multi-output call.
Once, after the full exact sum.
Once per tap.

hints.text: Add 16384 to the complete accumulator with daddiu.
Accumulators 16384, -16384 and -16385 become 32768, zero and -1 before shifting.

steps.title: Use an arithmetic shift for floor division

quiz.prompt: What does biased value -1 produce after this shift?

choices.text: Zero.

hints.text: Shift t0 right arithmetically by fifteen with dsra.
The three tie-adjacent recipes produce rounded codes one, zero and -1. The maximum eight-product sum produces 262144 before saturation.

steps.title: Test the rounded upper endpoint strictly

quiz.prompt: Does an exact rounded endpoint count as clipped?

choices.text: Yes, whenever it equals 32767.
No.
Only when the coefficients sum to one.

hints.text: Compare rounded t0 with 32767 using a strict signed test.
Rounded 262144 takes the high path with t9=1. Constant maximum input under the moving average gives 32767 with t9=0.

steps.title: Keep rounded in-range values on the store path

quiz.prompt: Which quantity determines clipping in this exercise?

choices.text: The sign of the first product.
The number of negative coefficients.
The complete rounded sample code.

hints.text: Test whether the rounded result is smaller than -32768.
Rounded -262136 takes the low path. Rounded -32768 and zero go to storage without increasing the count.

steps.title: Choose the positive endpoint

quiz.prompt: Why skip the following negative replacement?

choices.text: The return count is stored in the next label.
The two overflow directions need different endpoint values.
Both replacements must always execute.

hints.text: Load 32767 into t0, then transfer to the shared scalar_clipped label.
A large positive result becomes 32767 while v1 remains zero until the next count edit.

steps.title: Choose the negative endpoint

quiz.prompt: Can the final endpoint bytes alone reveal whether this path executed?

choices.text: Only when output is word aligned.
Yes; negative endpoints are always clipped.
No.

hints.text: Load -32768 into t0 for the lower-overflow path.
A large negative rounded result becomes -32768 with v1 still zero at the next unfinished region.

steps.title: Count one replacement per output

quiz.prompt: What unit does v1 count?

choices.text: Products outside halfword range.
Bytes written to the output.
Outputs whose rounded result needed saturation.

hints.text: Increment v1 at scalar_clipped.
Large positive and negative results each contribute one; exact rounded endpoints contribute zero.

steps.title: Write the first output byte only

quiz.prompt: Why would a word store violate this operation’s ownership?

choices.text: It reads the coefficient backwards.
It cannot represent a positive endpoint.
It changes bytes beyond the two-byte sample.

hints.text: Store the result’s low byte at a2 with sb.
Positive saturation writes ff as its first byte; negative saturation writes 00. The second byte remains a5.

steps.title: Complete the low-byte-first halfword

quiz.prompt: Why can this byte-extraction shift be logical?

choices.text: It replaces the earlier rounding operation.
Only the next selected byte is stored.
Negative output codes have no high bits.

hints.text: Shift the result right by eight into t1 and store that register’s low byte at a2+1.
Positive saturation stores ff 7f; negative saturation stores 00 80. Each overflow contributes one event.

steps.title: Advance the outer input by one sample

quiz.prompt: Why advance the input by two rather than sixteen bytes?

choices.text: Each next output slides the eight-tap window by one sample.
The window has only one input byte.
The coefficients advance automatically with a0.

hints.text: Advance a0 and a2 by two, consume one output and repeat scalar_window while count remains.

The default sixteen-output impulse returns eight samples of 2000 then zeros. The asymmetric two-output fixture yields 4096 then 3584. Sixty-four maximum positive sums return sixty-four clipping events.

steps.title: Inspect the provided vector quantizer before switching

quiz.prompt: What must the vector reduction supply to the provided postprocessing?

choices.text: One exact complete accumulator in t0.
Only the low word of a pair sum.
Eight separately rounded halfwords.

hints.text: The vector path already contains the rounding, bounds, endpoint replacement, counting and byte stores just developed in the scalar path.
The vector postprocessing advances a0 by two, keeps the coefficient base, and repeats fir_window. It applies one bias and arithmetic shift after each complete sum.

steps.title: Switch the public entry to the vector path

quiz.prompt: Does switching the public entry remove the scalar comparison function?

choices.text: No; it remains available under fir_scalar.
Yes; its completed code must be discarded.
Only when the input history is zero.

hints.text: Replace the provisional tail transfer to fir_scalar with the real fir_q15 entry: retain count, clear v1 and return at zero before coefficient setup.
Zero count returns without caller-data access. A one-output call reaches the unfinished coefficient load with v0=1, v1=0 and no output written.

steps.title: Load the coefficient window once

quiz.prompt: How many coefficient bytes does this load transfer?

choices.text: Two.
Eight.
Sixteen.

hints.text: Load all sixteen coefficient bytes into w1 before the output loop.
w1 contains all eight coefficient codes in stored oldest-first order.

steps.title: Build the coefficient sign-extension mask

quiz.prompt: Which halfwords must have an all-one high extension?

choices.text: The negative coefficients.
Only the coefficient at index seven.
Every coefficient with a nonzero low byte.

hints.text: Compare each signed halfword in w1 with zero.
For the mixed-sign recipe, mask lanes are ffff,0000,ffff,0000,ffff,0000,0000,0000.

steps.title: Widen the first four coefficient lanes

quiz.prompt: Which word represents coefficient -32768 correctly?

choices.text: ffff8000.

hints.text: Interleave w1’s low halfwords with their corresponding mask halfwords into w3.
w3’s words represent -32768,32767,-16384,16384; their raw hexadecimal patterns retain full signed extensions.

steps.title: Retain the other four widened coefficients

quiz.prompt: Which coefficient positions belong to this vector?

choices.text: Zero through three again.
Four through seven.
Eight through eleven.

hints.text: Use the high interleave to place coefficient positions four through seven in w4.
w4’s signed words are -1,1,0,4096.

steps.title: Load one complete eight-tap input window

quiz.prompt: Does count one authorize this sixteen-byte load?

choices.text: Only if the destination is also the source.
No; eight outputs are required.
Yes; its input includes seven history samples and one current sample.

hints.text: Load sixteen bytes from a0 into w0 for this output.
w0 holds the eight supplied sample codes, including history, in chronological order.

steps.title: Derive a fresh sign mask for the window

quiz.prompt: Why recompute this mask each output?

choices.text: The coefficient scale changes each call.
The input window changes.
A mask must always contain the clipping count.

hints.text: Compare each signed sample halfword with zero into w2.
The mixed-sign input mask is ffff,0000,ffff,0000,ffff,0000,0000,0000.

steps.title: Widen the first four input samples

quiz.prompt: Does widening multiply a sample by 65536?

choices.text: Yes; every new word shifts the code left.
Only for a negative sample.
No; correct sign extension preserves its numerical value.

hints.text: Interleave the low input halfwords with their sign masks into w5.

steps.title: Widen the final four input samples

quiz.prompt: Where is the current sample in this window?

choices.text: Outside the loaded sixteen bytes.
At position seven, the last widened input word.
At position zero.

hints.text: Use the high interleave for sample positions four through seven, producing w6.
w6’s signed words are -1,1,0,16000.

steps.title: Form two exact doubleword pair sums

quiz.prompt: Why not use dotp_s.w directly on the original halfwords?

choices.text: An allowed two-product sum can overflow its signed word result.
It would process no products.
It requires aligned output but otherwise gives the same exact sum.

hints.text: Apply dotp_s.d to the first four widened sample/coefficient words.
The mixed-sign fixture gives 2147418113 and 32768000 in w7. Minimum/minimum pairs give 2147483648 in each doubleword.

steps.title: Include the last four tap products

quiz.prompt: Which pair includes the current sample?

choices.text: Positions zero and one.
No pair; history alone determines output.
Positions six and seven.

hints.text: Apply dotp_s.d to w6 and w4, retaining pair sums for positions four/five and six/seven in w8.
The mixed-sign fixture gives 2 and 65536000 in w8. The extreme fixture again gives two positive 2147483648 sums.

steps.title: Combine the two halves without narrowing

quiz.prompt: How many partial sums remain after this vector addition?

choices.text: Eight halfword products.
One final rounded sample.
Two doubleword sums.

hints.text: Add w8 into w7 with addv.d.
The mixed-sign partial totals are 2147418115 and 98304000. The extreme fixture produces 4294967296 in each lane.

steps.title: Transfer the first doubleword partial sum

quiz.prompt: What would a word-sized copy lose in the extreme fixture?

choices.text: The bit above the low thirty-two positions.
The coefficient array address.
Only redundant sign bits.

hints.text: Copy w7[0] into t0 with copy_s.d.
t0 is 2147418115 for the mixed-sign fixture and 4294967296 for the extreme fixture.

steps.title: Transfer the second doubleword partial sum

quiz.prompt: Which products would be omitted if t1 were ignored?

choices.text: Two,three,six,seven.
Only product seven.
All products from the first input half.

hints.text: Copy w7[1] into t1 while retaining the first sum in t0.
The mixed-sign fixture has t0=2147418115 and t1=98304000.

steps.title: Enter the proven quantizer with one exact sum

quiz.prompt: When is rounding allowed in this path?

choices.text: After the final exact scalar addition.
Before sign-extending the input words.
After each vector pair sum.

hints.text: Add t1 into t0 with daddu.

The mixed-sign total is 2245722115 before the provided quantizer and clips positively. The maximum total is 8589934592. Default and sixty-four-output fixtures now finish with correct samples and counts.

steps.title: Read the caller’s completed results at their boundary

quiz.prompt: Which state still contains 99 at filter_ready?

choices.text: The returned output count.
The two caller result words.
Every output sample.

hints.text: Restore the default input and count sixteen after construction.
At results_ready, processed=16 and clipped=0; output is eight halfwords 2000 followed by eight zeros.

steps.title: Distinguish rounding from a clipping event

quiz.prompt: Should raw value -32768.5 count as clipped under this contract?

choices.text: No; its rounded code is -32768.
Only when a vector register holds it.
Yes; any raw value below -32768 must clip.

hints.text: Use the documented negative halfway accumulator -1073758208.
The halfway case returns the negative endpoint with zero clips; the rounded -32769 case returns the same endpoint with one clip.

steps.title: Repeat a stream with explicit chunk history

quiz.prompt: Why does the second input begin at original sample position twenty-four?

choices.text: That starts the next window with its seven required history samples.
Every output consumes eight new input samples.
The next call discards history automatically.

hints.text: Split a sixty-four-output input after output twenty-three.
The concatenated result equals a complete call. The checks verify all sixty-five cuts, including an empty first or second call, in one session.

steps.title: Grade behavior separately from the illustrated temporaries

quiz.prompt: May a free-writing submission omit fir_scalar?

choices.text: Only if it reproduces the example’s instruction count.
Yes; only the public fir_q15 entry and supplied harness are required.
No; every private comparison label is part of the interface.

hints.text: Construction observations name registers so this particular sequence can be explained and checked.
Both a scalar implementation and the widened-vector implementation satisfy the same final contract. Correct argument-register changes after last use are accepted.

steps.title: Compare the stored input and filtered audio

quiz.prompt: Does this prove the low input passed through unchanged?

choices.text: Yes; removing a high component cannot affect any other sample.
Only because the sample rate is sixteen thousand.
No; the comparison is with the filtered low component.

hints.text: Use the low, high and mixed listening scenes with their explicit periodic histories.
Both implementations produce identical six-file audio sets. High-only output is zero PCM; the filtered mixed and low files are byte-identical.

quiz.prompt: What work remains in the vector input path?

choices.text: Repeated reads of the seven shared samples in adjacent windows.
No input reads after the first window.
A mandatory reload of all coefficients per output.

hints.text: Read the table for quiet inputs.
The measurements describe these implementations and inputs. They do not establish host elapsed time or an instruction-count grading requirement.

steps.title: Explore another strategy under the same arithmetic rule

quiz.prompt: Which change requires a new arithmetic specification?

choices.text: Retaining read-only coefficients in registers.
Choosing another temporary register.
Changing the coefficient scale or tap count.

hints.text: Try caching coefficients in a scalar implementation or retaining part of the vector window between outputs.
An optimization is accepted when it preserves the public behavior, including negative ties, large sums, clipping counts and chunk continuity.
